lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Did you know Moerichis, Diogenes? The rich one — very rich — from Corinth, the one with all the merchant ships? His cousin was Aristeas, also rich. The two of them used to quote that Homeric line at each other: 'kill me or I'll kill you first.'

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: They were the same age, and each one was cultivating the other for the inheritance. They made their wills publicly — Moerichis leaving everything to Aristeas if he went first, Aristeas leaving everything to Moerichis if he went first. That was the arrangement in writing. In practice they were in constant competition over who could flatter the other more. And the soothsayers — the ones who read the stars, the ones who read dreams, the Chaldean types — even the Pythian oracle itself kept changing its verdict: now Aristeas had the edge, now Moerichis. The balance of all those talents kept tipping back and forth between them.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And how did it end? I want to hear this.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: They both died. Same day. And both estates passed to Eunomius and Thrasydes — cousins of theirs who had never once consulted an oracle about any of this, and had no reason to expect it. They were sailing from Sicyon to Cirrha and in the middle of the crossing they ran into a squall off the Iapyx and capsized.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Excellent. [pause] You know, when we were alive, we never had thoughts like that about each other. I never once prayed for Antisthenes to die so I could inherit his walking stick — and it was a very good one, he'd made it from wild olive — and I don't imagine you ever lay awake coveting my estate when I was gone: the tub, the knapsack, two cups of lupine seeds.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: I had no use for any of that. And neither did you, Diogenes. What actually needed inheriting — you got from Antisthenes, and I got from you. Worth considerably more than the Persian empire.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Wisdom. Self-sufficiency. Truth. Plain speaking. Freedom.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Yes. I remember taking on that fortune from Antisthenes and leaving you an even larger share of it.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Everyone else ignored that kind of wealth entirely. Nobody cultivated us in hopes of an inheritance. All eyes were on the gold.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Naturally. They had nowhere to put what we had to offer — they'd been so thoroughly softened by luxury that they leaked, like a rotten purse. You could pour wisdom into them, frankness, truth — it fell straight out the bottom. Nothing to hold it. The same thing that happens to the daughters of Danaus, hauling water into that punctured jar. The gold, though — that they guarded with their teeth and nails and every means available.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: So here we are, still rich. [pause] And the others will arrive with one obol each — and only keep that as far as the ferryman.
